TP63 acts as a transcriptional activator at the HNRNPA1 regulatory region, so reducing TP63 removes a positive input to the gene: TP63 loss → decreased occupancy/activation at the HNRNPA1 promoter-enhancer → lower HNRNPA1 transcription → lower steady-state HNRNPA1 mRNA and hnRNPA1 protein than in the matched unperturbed control. The key mediator is the TP63-dependent transactivation of the HNRNPA1 locus — no intermediate signaling step is required, the order is simply TP63 depletion first, then loss of activating drive, then a drop in HNRNPA1 output. (This assumes the annotated regulation is activating, which is the default reading of "regulated by"; if the relationship were instead repressive, the direction would invert.)

TET2 is a TET-family dioxygenase that converts 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) and thereby licenses active, stepwise DNA demethylation at CpG-rich regulatory elements. Loss of TET2 function therefore shifts the locus toward 5mC accumulation, i.e., hypermethylation. The ELOVL2 promoter/first-exon CpG island is one of the most methylation-sensitive regulatory regions in the genome (it is the canonical marker in DNA-methylation "age clocks"), and its methylation state is inversely coupled to transcription. With TET2 reduced, that region gains 5mC, chromatin accessibility and transcription-factor occupancy fall, and the upstream activator ESR1 — which is required for ELOVL2 transcription — can no longer productively engage its binding site. The causal order is thus: TET2 loss → loss of 5hmC/5mC demethylation at the ELOVL2 regulatory region → promoter/enhancer hypermethylation and reduced accessibility → decreased ESR1 recruitment → reduced ELOVL2 transcription. The effect is mediated through the ESR1 axis rather than through any direct action of TET2 on the ELOVL2 gene body, so the net expectation is a decrease in ELOVL2 expression relative to the matched unperturbed control.

GATA1 D218G is a Diamond–Blackfan anemia–associated missense change in the N-terminal zinc finger, a domain that mediates cofactor (FOG1/ZFPM1, TAL1) recruitment and modulates DNA binding and transactivation; the mutant behaves as a hypomorphic/loss-of-function allele, so functional GATA1 activity at its target loci falls. Because GATA1 acts as an activator of Lrrc39 (an erythroid-enriched, GATA1-bound target), the causal order runs: variant → impaired N-finger function and weakened cofactor-dependent transactivation → reduced GATA1 occupancy/activation at the Lrrc39 regulatory region → decreased Lrrc39 transcription. Net effect relative to the matched unperturbed control: Lrrc39 mRNA goes down.

GREB1 is a canonical estrogen-receptor target gene: ESR1 (ERα) binds estrogen-response elements in the GREB1 promoter/enhancer and drives its transcription, so GREB1 mRNA is a direct readout of ESR1 activity. The perturbation here reduces GREB1 itself (loss-or-reduction of GREB1e), which removes GREB1 transcript directly, and it also interrupts the positive feedback arm in which GREB1 co-activates ESR1-dependent transcription — so the receptor-driven input is not restored. Because the causal order runs ESR1 → GREB1, knocking down GREB1 at the effector end cannot raise its own output; the matched control retains full ESR1-driven GREB1 transcription, so the perturbed sample sits below it. Net expectation: GREB1 expression goes down.

Loss of ESR1 removes the transcriptional activator that sits on the SMAD7 locus, so SMAD7 output falls. Mechanistically, ESR1 (ERα) occupies estrogen-response/AP-1–Sp1 elements in the SMAD7 promoter and recruits p160/SRC coactivators and RNA Pol II to drive SMAD7 transcription; it additionally sustains SMAD7 transcript levels post-transcriptionally through ER-dependent p38 MAPK–Smad7 signaling. Order of events: ESR1 depletion → loss of promoter occupancy and coactivator recruitment → reduced SMAD7 mRNA synthesis and stability → lower SMAD7 protein, which in turn de-represses TGF-β/Smad2/3 signaling (the feedback arm SMAD7 normally restrains). Because both arms act in the same direction, net SMAD7 expression moves down relative to the matched untreated control.

BHLHE40 is not acting as a repressor of Hmgcs2 here — it behaves as a required co-factor of the PPARα transcriptional complex. In hepatocytes, BHLHE40 occupies the same hepatic enhancer clusters as PPARα and its obligate partner RXRα (and HNF4), where it physically associates with RXRα and PPARα coactivators/corepressors, and its binding sites sit near PPARα-driven metabolic genes such as Hmgcs2, the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis. Order of events: BHLHE40 loss (siRNA/knockdown) → weakened coactivator recruitment and enhancer activity at the Hmgcs2 regulatory region → reduced PPARα-dependent transactivation → lower Hmgcs2 mRNA. Consistent with this, Bhlhe40 knockdown in primary hepatocytes blunts induction of PPARα target genes by the PPARα agonist WY-14643, with Hmgcs2 among the most strongly affected genes, whereas BHLHE40 overexpression does the opposite. So relative to the matched unperturbed control, Hmgcs2 expression is expected to go down — the PPARα→Hmgcs2 axis is attenuated through loss of a BHLHE40-dependent coactivator input rather than derepression.

ZNF143 acts as a transcriptional activator that binds promoter-proximal SBS (SPH) motifs and is required for efficient recruitment/assembly of the transcription preinitiation complex. Because AP1S3 sits downstream of ZNF143 in this regulatory relationship, reducing ZNF143 (CRISPRi knockdown, siRNA/shRNA depletion, or loss-of-function) lowers ZNF143 occupancy at the AP1S3 regulatory region, which reduces RNA polymerase II loading and productive initiation at that promoter. The order is therefore: ZNF143 loss → decreased promoter occupancy and PIC/Pol II recruitment → reduced AP1S3 transcription → lower steady-state AP1S3 mRNA, and ultimately lower AP1S3 protein, relative to the matched unperturbed control.

H2A.Z (H2AFZ), deposited by the SRCAP and EP400/p400 complexes, is enriched at promoters and enhancers where it forms a less stable nucleosome that keeps regulatory DNA accessible and poised for factor binding. TP63 (p63) requires this open, H2A.Z-marked chromatin to occupy its response elements on SAMD9L; H2A.Z loss therefore destabilizes the +1/regulatory nucleosomes and reduces p63 residence at those sites. With diminished p63 occupancy, the activating input to SAMD9L transcription falls, so SAMD9L mRNA decreases. Order of events: H2A.Z depletion → reduced nucleosome eviction/accessibility at the SAMD9L locus → loss of TP63 binding to its regulatory elements → reduced SAMD9L transcription.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator that binds its cognate motif (the "ZNF143/SPH" element, typically CCAYTAGCTGC or related) at promoters and enhancers and recruits the general transcription machinery and co-activators (e.g., p300/CBP, SPT-family and mediator components) to drive transcription. CCDC92 is listed as a direct, positively regulated target, and the causal chain runs ZNF143 occupancy → productive initiation/elongation at the CCDC92 promoter → mRNA output. Removing or reducing ZNF143 therefore releases that activation, so steady-state CCDC92 mRNA (and protein) falls relative to the matched unperturbed control: loss of activator → loss of transactivation → decreased CCDC92 expression, i.e., down.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific C2H2 zinc-finger transcriptional activator that binds Staf-binding sites (SBS) in the promoters of most of its activated targets, and CRCP sits in that class of promoter-proximal, ZNF143-bound genes. Mechanistically, ZNF143 acts at the initiation step: it occupies the promoter, recruits/anchors cofactors and general transcription machinery (e.g., SNAPc, POU-domain partners, HCFC1–THAP11, and cohesin/CTCF-linked looping), and thereby licenses RNA polymerase II initiation. When ZNF143 is depleted, that activating input is removed at the CRCP promoter, so initiation efficiency falls and CRCP mRNA (and consequently protein) declines relative to the matched unperturbed control — i.e., reduced transcription first, then reduced steady-state CRCP levels. The ordering matters: the primary event is loss of ZNF143 binding and decreased Pol II initiation at CRCP, and the lower CRCP expression is the downstream readout, not an indirect secondary repression. (Caveat: ZNF143 is context-specific and directly represses a minority of genes through promoter occlusion — for those, depletion raises expression. CRCP falls in the activator category unless a specific dataset shows the reverse.)

ZNF143 (zinc-finger protein 143, also known as SBF/Staf) is a sequence-specific activator: it recognizes its SBS consensus motif in target promoters — frequently CpG island promoters, often in concert with SP1/CTCF at shared regulatory modules — and its transactivation domain delivers coactivators that drive RNA polymerase II recruitment and productive elongation. Removing ZNF143 therefore removes a positive input rather than relieving a brake: the proximal promoter loses occupancy, coactivator/Pol II loading at the ENKD1 locus falls, and the rate of ENKD1 transcription drops, so steady-state ENKD1 mRNA declines relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same cell context. Order of events: ZNF143 loss → loss of promoter/motif occupancy and coactivator recruitment → reduced Pol II initiation/elongation → decreased ENKD1 transcription → lower ENKD1 expression. The inference assumes the annotated regulatory link is activating in nature; were the mechanism repression (ZNF143 acting as a silencer at this locus), the expected direction would invert.

ZNF143 (also known as SBF/Staf) acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional activator: it binds its cognate motif — the "SBS"/ZNF143 consensus element, often found at promoters and enhancers — and recruits coactivators and general transcription machinery to drive RNA polymerase II initiation. Because GOLGA2 is a direct ZNF143 target, loss or reduction of ZNF143 removes this activating input at the GOLGA2 locus; the order of events is (1) reduced ZNF143 protein available for chromatin binding, (2) diminished occupancy and coactivator recruitment at the GOLGA2 regulatory region, (3) decreased Pol II initiation/elongation, and consequently (4) lower GOLGA2 mRNA relative to the matched unperturbed control. The key mediator is therefore ZNF143 itself acting as the positive regulator, with no compensatory activation expected — so the direction is down, not up.

ZNF143 (also called SBF/STAF) acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional activator that binds promoter-proximal elements and supports RNA polymerase II recruitment and promoter–enhancer looping. In this loss-of-reduction setting, removing ZNF143 lowers its occupancy at the JUN promoter, so the activating input to JUN is lost; the immediate consequence is reduced JUN transcription, followed downstream by lower JUN mRNA and JUN/AP-1 protein and reduced activity of its target program. The key mediator is therefore the ZNF143-dependent promoter activation complex, and the order is: ZNF143 loss → decreased promoter occupancy/activation → decreased JUN transcription → lower JUN expression. No compensatory feedback strong enough to invert the sign is expected in the matched control comparison, so the direction is down.

ZNF143 is a zinc-finger, sequence-specific transcriptional activator that binds SPH/Staf-type motifs in the promoters of its target genes and stimulates their transcription. In this context it acts as an upstream activator of MED16; when ZNF143 is lost or reduced, its occupancy at the MED16 promoter is diminished, which weakens the recruitment/assembly of the pre-initiation complex and RNA polymerase II at that promoter. The order is therefore: ZNF143 depletion → loss of activating promoter occupancy at MED16 → reduced transcription initiation/elongation → fewer MED16 transcripts. The key mediator here is ZNF143 itself functioning as the trans-acting activator whose loss removes positive regulation, so MED16 mRNA is expected to fall relative to the matched unperturbed control.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator: it binds its cognate motif in the NUTF2 promoter and recruits coactivator/Mediator machinery that promotes RNA polymerase II initiation. Under a loss-or-reduction perturbation of ZNF143, that activating occupancy at the NUTF2 promoter is lost, so the promoter's transcriptional output falls and NUTF2 mRNA levels decline relative to the matched unperturbed control. The causal order is: ZNF143 depletion → loss of activator binding/coactivator recruitment at the NUTF2 promoter → reduced Pol II transcription → decreased NUTF2 expression (mRNA, then protein).

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator, not a repressor: it occupies a conserved motif in the promoters of its target genes and acts as a looping/scaffolding factor that helps bring distal regulatory elements into proximity with the promoter, promoting RNA polymerase II recruitment and productive elongation. In the loss-of-reduction arm, the primary event is removal of ZNF143 protein from the PRKAA2 promoter; the immediate consequence is loss of that activation and looping support, so the PRKAA2 locus shifts to a less accessible, lower-initiation state, and PRKAA2 mRNA is subsequently lost at a slower turnover-driven rate. The causal order is therefore ZNF143 loss → promoter de-occupancy and reduced chromatin looping/Pol II loading → decreased PRKAA2 transcription → lower steady-state PRKAA2 expression relative to the matched unperturbed control. Any indirect feedback through AMPK signalling (e.g. altered AMPK activity changing cellular energy state) is a downstream, secondary effect and would not reverse the direction of the direct regulatory loss.

ZNF143 is a zinc-finger, CTCF-like promoter-anchoring factor that acts as a transcriptional activator, typically binding the ~18-bp SBS motif in the promoters of constitutively expressed, housekeeping-type genes such as RIC8A. Loss or reduction of ZNF143 removes that activation: it first reduces promoter occupancy and the associated coactivator/RNAP II recruitment at the RIC8A promoter, which lowers the rate of RIC8A transcription and, consequently, steady-state RIC8A mRNA and protein levels. Because ZNF143 acts upstream at the promoter, the effect on the target is direct and immediate, so within the same matched context RIC8A expression is expected to decrease relative to the unperturbed control.

ZNF143 is a transcriptional activator, not a repressor: it binds a specific recognition element (the ZNF143/SPH-type site) in the promoters of its target genes and drives their transcription, typically by recruiting coactivators and helping maintain an open, accessible promoter. So the causal chain here runs: ZNF143 loss/reduction → the SAV1 promoter is no longer occupied (or is occupied far less) by ZNF143 → activating input to that promoter is lost → SAV1 transcription decreases → steady-state SAV1 mRNA, and downstream SAV1 protein, fall. The key mediator is ZNF143 binding at the SAV1 promoter itself; the ordering matters because the drop in SAV1 is a consequence of losing the trans-activating factor, not a compensatory response. This direction is what a direct-activation model predicts for SAV1 as a ZNF143 target, which aligns with ZNF143's established role as a promoter-bound activator rather than a silencer — if instead the evidence showed ZNF143 acting as a repressor at this locus (a minority of contexts), the expectation would flip, so the predicted "down" rests on the activator relationship you specified.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcription factor that binds promoter and enhancer regions and acts as a transcriptional activator, so its binding at the SNRNP48 locus is what drives (or helps maintain) SNRNP48 transcription. Reducing ZNF143 levels lowers the occupancy of its cognate motif in the SNRNP48 regulatory region, which in turn reduces recruitment of coactivators and RNA polymerase II and drops the rate of SNRNP48 mRNA synthesis. Because the causal chain runs ZNF143 → promoter/enhancer occupancy → SNRNP48 transcription, the loss-of-function perturbation is expected to decrease SNRNP48 expression rather than increase it. The effect should appear within the timeframe of transcription and mature-mRNA turnover of SNRNP48 (i.e., the protein's own half-life is not relevant, since the mediator here is transcriptional output of the target gene).

ZNF143 (also called SBF/STAF) acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional activator: it binds its motif in target promoters and recruits coactivators/general machinery to promote RNA polymerase II initiation, and it also supports promoter–enhancer looping. In this causal chain, ZNF143 binds the THOC7 regulatory region and drives its transcription; reducing ZNF143 removes that activation input, so the promoter fires less efficiently and THOC7 mRNA levels fall. Order: loss of ZNF143 protein → reduced occupancy at the THOC7 promoter → decreased initiation/elongation by RNA Pol II → lower steady-state THOC7 expression. The matched unperturbed control keeps the activator in place, so the perturbed sample is the lower of the two.

ZNF143 (also known as SBF/Staf) is a sequence-specific activator that binds the highly conserved "SPH" motif (GCCNNNGGC) in promoters and enhancers and drives transcription, largely by anchoring chromatin-looping complexes in which it contacts cohesin and the Mediator-associated SMC1/STAG components. Since the regulatory relationship given here is activating (ZNF143 acting as an activator at the TPRA1 locus), the causal order is: ZNF143 protein is depleted → its SPH element at the TPRA1 promoter/enhancer loses occupancy → the promoter-enhancer looping and coactivator recruitment that depended on ZNF143 is lost → RNA Pol II initiation/output at TPRA1 falls. The key mediator is therefore loss of ZNF143-dependent promoter-enhancer looping and coactivator recruitment. Net expectation: the matched unperturbed control will show higher TPRA1 transcript, so the perturbed sample goes **down** relative to it. (The magnitude depends on whether TPRA1's SPH element is the dominant regulatory input in that cell type; if the site is a minor contributor, the drop may be modest rather than absent.)

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator of RNA polymerase II promoters (it binds the SBS/SPH motif, "ACTACAATTCCC"), so it acts as a positive regulator rather than a repressor. Reducing ZNF143 therefore removes an activating input at the ZFTA locus: the causal order runs ZNF143 loss → decreased promoter occupancy and loss of transcriptional activation at the ZFTA regulatory region → reduced RNA polymerase II initiation/elongation → lower ZFTA mRNA. Because the perturbation is loss-of-function of a positive regulator, the target moves in the same direction as the regulator, i.e., down relative to the matched unperturbed control; the effect would be attenuated or reversed only if ZNF143 were acting indirectly through a repressive intermediary, which is not the mode assumed here. (This assumes the regulation is direct and activating; if ZFTA were instead repressed by ZNF143 — e.g., via an indirect loop — the expectation would flip to up.)

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator: it binds SBS/SPH motifs in promoters and enhancers and recruits co-activators (e.g., the SBF/STAF complex and general transcription machinery) to drive transcription of its target genes. Because ZNF473 is a direct ZNF143 target, reducing ZNF143 lowers the occupancy of ZNF473's regulatory region by its activating factor, which decreases the rate of ZNF473 transcription and consequently its steady-state mRNA level. The causal order is: ZNF143 loss → reduced activator binding at the ZNF473 locus → less transcriptional initiation/elongation → ZNF473 mRNA down, with no compensatory repression release expected since ZNF143 is not acting as a repressor at this gene.

up.

POU5F1/OCT4 acts as a direct repressor of PAX6 rather than an activator: in the pluripotent state OCT4 (with NANOG/SOX2) occupies the PAX6 promoter — including the P1 region overlapping the first exon — and holds the locus in a silent, poorly accessible state. Reducing POU5F1 removes that promoter-bound repression first, which de-represses the PAX6 locus and, via chromatin remodeling (nucleosome depletion at the PAX6 promoter by BAF/SNF5-containing complexes) and opening of the promoter, allows PAX6 transcription to initiate; PAX6 mRNA and protein therefore rise as cells exit pluripotency toward neuroectoderm. Order: OCT4 loss → loss of promoter occupancy/de-repression → chromatin opening at PAX6 → increased PAX6 transcription and protein.

up

TGF-β/SMAD3 activation drives the answer: ligand-bound TGF-β receptors phosphorylate SMAD2/3, and the resulting SMAD3–SMAD4 complex binds the PTPRK regulatory region to transactivate it, so PTPRK mRNA rises above the matched unperturbed control. NOTCH1 activation is the upstream/coperating input — Notch signaling feeds into and amplifies TGF-β/SMAD3-dependent transcription (and the two pathways converge on shared cofactors), placing NOTCH1 above SMAD3 and SMAD3 directly above PTPRK in the chain. Because the intervention is a gain/activation rather than a loss, the net effect on PTPRK is positive rather than the decrease seen with SMAD3 inhibition.

up

UHRF1 is the epigenetic effector of a PPARA-driven repression arm, and Smpd3 sits directly downstream of it. Under basal/agonized PPARA signaling, PPARA autoinduces itself, transactivates E2f8 through a PPRE in its intron 1, and E2F8 then drives Uhrf1 transcription (PPARA has no binding peak in the Uhrf1 promoter, so the step is indirect). UHRF1, together with DNMT1 and HDAC1, is recruited to the H3K9me3-marked Smpd3 promoter, where it deposits 5-methylcytosine and maintains a closed, silenced chromatin state — Smpd3 (nSMase2) therefore sits repressed. Removing UHRF1 breaks this chain at its final step: the DNMT1/HDAC1 complex is no longer tethered to the promoter, promoter methylation and H3K9me3 are lost, and the brake on Smpd3 is released. The order is PPARA → E2F8 → UHRF1 → Smpd3 promoter methylation → repression; knock down UHRF1 (shUhrf1, or shE2f8 upstream of it) and Smpd3 mRNA de-represses relative to the matched shRNA-control in the same PPARA-agonist-treated liver context, so the direction is up.

The E-box at chr17_BS377 (CACGTG) is a MYC binding element, and MYC acts as a transcriptional activator at such sites — it binds the E-box through its bHLH-LZ domain, recruits coactivator complexes (e.g., TRRAP/STAGA and associated HAT activity), and drives RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription. Perturbing the site breaks that binding event, so the immediate consequence is loss of MYC occupancy at this regulatory element, followed by reduced coactivator recruitment and lower transcriptional output at the PFAS locus. Since PFAS (phosphoribosylformylglycinamidine synthase, a core purine-biosynthesis gene) is a direct MYC-amplified target in this context, the matched unperturbed control maintains MYC-driven activation and the perturbed condition does not — giving a relative decrease. The causal order is therefore: E-box disruption → loss of MYC binding → dismantled activation complex → reduced PFAS transcription → lower PFAS expression.

FOXK1 does not act on RPS16 by itself — it works as a required co-factor of TP63, sitting on the accessory anchors of p63-dependent enhancer–promoter loops. RPS16 is a TP63-*activated* target (part of the p63-driven proliferative/ribosome-biogenesis program), so its transcription depends on those loops staying closed. When FOXK1 is lost, the p63-bound enhancer can no longer be brought into contact with the RPS16 promoter: the p63-dependent loop weakens, TP63 occupancy no longer translates into productive transcription, and RPS16 mRNA falls toward baseline. Order of events: FOXK1 loss → loss of the FOXK1-p63 looping complex at the RPS16 enhancer → reduced TP63-dependent promoter engagement → lower RPS16 expression.

down

The ATP2B4 intron 1 element is a GATA1-bound erythroid enhancer: GATA1 occupies its WGATAR-type motif and, with cofactors (CBP/p300, MED12/Mediator), maintains local chromatin accessibility and loops the enhancer onto the ATP2B4 promoter to drive PMCA4 transcription. Perturbing (deleting or mutating) that intronic site removes the GATA1 docking platform first, so GATA1 occupancy and enhancer-associated marks (H3K27ac, ATAC signal) collapse, enhancer–promoter looping and coactivator recruitment fall away next, and transcriptional initiation at the ATP2B4 promoter consequently drops. Because the matched control retains the intact GATA1-activated enhancer, ATP2B4 expression in the perturbed context is expected to go down, not up.

down

miR-451 is the effector arm of the GATA1→miR-144/451 axis: GATA1 transactivates the miR-144/451 locus, and the mature miR-451 is loaded into AGO2-RISC, whose seed-paired site in the Ywhaz 3'UTR recruits GW182/TNRC6 to repress translation and trigger deadenylation and decay of the transcript. So the order runs GATA1 → pri-miR-451 → mature miR-451 → Ywhaz 3'UTR targeting → reduced Ywhaz mRNA and 14-3-3ζ protein. Because the perturbation is gain/activation of the microRNA rather than of the transcription factor, the net effect on Ywhaz relative to the matched unperturbed control is downward — and this repression is post-transcriptional, so it can be visible even while GATA1-driven transcription of the locus continues.

up

miR-181b is a STAT3-induced microRNA that acts post-transcriptionally on CYLD: it base-pairs with the CYLD 3′UTR and recruits the RISC/Argonaute machinery, which both blocks translation and accelerates CYLD mRNA decay, holding CYLD protein at a low steady state. When miR-181b is lost or reduced, that repression is relieved, so CYLD mRNA and protein rise — the effect is fast (loss of an existing repressor) and does not require new transcription. Order and mediators: active STAT3 drives miR-181b expression → miR-181b represses CYLD — knock down miR-181b → CYLD de-repression (up). Note the downstream consequence: CYLD is a deubiquitinase that strips K63-linked ubiquitin from NEMO/TRAF and other NF-κB pathway components, damping NF-κB and STAT3 signaling, so the CYLD increase tends to feed back and further lower miR-181b, reinforcing the same direction.

down

FOSL1 (FRA-1) acts upstream as an AP-1 component that supports ETV4 — the two factors co-occupy composite ETS/AP-1 regulatory elements and FOSL1-ETV4 show positively correlated, mutually reinforcing expression. Because NOTCH4 is a direct transcriptional activation target of ETV4 (ETV4/PEA3 binds the NOTCH4 regulatory region and drives its transcription; siRNA against ETV4 lowers NOTCH4 mRNA), the loss or reduction of FOSL1 is expected to relax this activating input, first lowering ETV4-dependent transactivation at the NOTCH4 locus and then reducing steady-state NOTCH4 transcript. Order of events: FOSL1 loss → decreased ETV4 activity/abundance → diminished ETV4 occupancy and activation at the NOTCH4 promoter → NOTCH4 expression decreases relative to the matched unperturbed control.
